items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He introduced me to Claude Hopkins, he introduced me to Buck and Bubbles

ctx.x: Do you remember some of the other groups you heard, bands you heard right on that first couple of days when you arrived?

Art Tatum…I walked up 7th Avenue and there was Ellington walking up the street and the next thing you know Claude Hopkins is walking up the street. Louis Armstrong, I’d see him on 7th Avenue. They’d all walk up and down 7th Avenue. Oh man, I said, gee, can you top this? I’m standing there just looking at them because most of the times I had seen them was on the stage and I’m out in the audience and here I am just about ready to shake his hand. Oh my goodness. After you get through work, you go up to Monroe’s…
Were you sitting in much or just listening?

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Yeah, Claude Hopkins, Duke, Earl Hines, Fletcher. That was the piano players era for bands.

ctx.x: That's right, there was Claude Hopkins.
Yeah, Claude Hopkins, Duke, Earl Hines, Fletcher. That was the piano players era for bands. Except Louie Armstrong. He was always a band leader.

But piano players, well they would seem more likely to have a band because they could sit from the piano, they could direct. You take an instrumentalist, you'd have to hire two of what you were playing. Like if the band leader was a tenor player, they'd have to hire another tenor player. If the band leader was a trumpet player, they'd have to have another one. But the piano player, you wouldn't have to hire nobody else. So automatically, he would become the bandleader, the director, you know.
